findings.title: order() added as abstract method breaks third-party CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: The new `int order()` method on the public `CryptoProvider` interface has no default implementation. Any existing external implementation of `CryptoProvider` (e.g. custom providers used by downstream projects or the adapter SPI consumers) will fail to load at runtime once keycloak-common is upgraded: ServiceLoader instantiation throws ServiceConfigurationError with AbstractMethodError on first call to order(), or the class no longer compiles. Since CryptoProvider already uses `default` methods elsewhere in this same interface (getSupportedKeyStoreTypes, getSupportedRsaKeySizes), `order()` should be declared as `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) to preserve binary and source compatibility.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default JKS KeyStore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: The implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which on a stock JVM is the Sun provider (for "pkcs12"/"jks"), not BouncyCastle. The interface contract ("@return BouncyCastle security provider") is violated, and any code path in keycloak-core/authz-client that calls `CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider()` expecting BC-specific behavior (e.g. algorithms only BC provides, or null-check semantics used by WildFlyElytronProvider consumers) will silently get a wrong provider. Either return null (as WildFlyElytronProvider does when no BC is available) or document why the default keystore provider is acceptable here.

findings.title: Dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER creates and discards encoder objects
findings.body: Lines 114-115 (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) build two encoders whose results are thrown away; only the `writeDerSeq` chain on lines 117-121 is used. This is leftover debugging/dead code that allocates needless objects on every signature conversion and confuses readers into thinking those calls have an effect. The two lines should be removed.

findings.title: readSequence() silently accepts indefinite-length encodings and returns an empty list
findings.body: When readLength() encounters the indefinite-length marker 0x80 it returns -1; readSequence()'s `while (length > 0)` loop then never executes and an empty list is returned without consuming any content octets. Callers like asn1derToConcatenatedRS will only detect this indirectly via the size!=2 check, but any future caller iterating the returned list would treat a malformed BER indefinite-length sequence as a valid empty sequence instead of receiving an error. Indefinite length should be rejected explicitly (it is not valid DER).

findings.title: integerToBytes silently truncates out-of-range signature integers
findings.body: In asn1derToConcatenatedRS, integerToBytes keeps only the low `qLength` bytes when the decoded BigInteger is longer than the expected half-signature length (`qLength < bytes.length` branch takes the *last* bytes of toByteArray(), which for a positive value drops the most significant bytes). A DER signature whose r or s exceeds the curve order would be silently accepted and mangled rather than rejected, producing a signature that could verify against a different value than what was signed in length-mismatch scenarios. Validation (throwing when the value does not fit in qLength) would be the safe behavior for signature conversion.
